13ca327def9d.source_text: FDA Review Violations were identified and documented during review of your drug manufacturing facility, Guangdong Bangze Medicine Co., Ltd., FDA Establishment Identifier (FEI) 3035364398. This review was conducted under FDA’s statutory authority and public health responsibilities to protect the public from unsafe, ineffective, and poor quality drugs. Your facility is registered with the FDA as a manufacturer of over-the-counter (OTC) drug products. FDA has reviewed the records you submitted in response to our January 20, 2026, request and subsequent correspondence, for records and other information pursuant to section 704(a)(4) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) for your facility. This warning letter summarizes significant violations of Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) regulations for finished pharmaceuticals. See Title 21 Code of Federal Regulations, parts 210 and 211 (21 CFR, parts 210 and 211). Because your methods, facilities, or controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding of drugs as described in your response to our 704(a)(4) request, do not conform to CGMP, your drug products are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B)). Violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act The following are violations identified during our review. As a reminder, this is not an all-inclusive list of violations at your facility. 1. Your firm failed to test samples of each component for identity and conformity with all appropriate written specifications for purity, strength, and quality (21 CFR 211.84(d)(1) and 211.84(d)(2)). Your firm manufactures OTC drug products including (b)(4) . Based on the records and information you provided, you did not demonstrate that you adequately tested the identity, purity, or strength of components used in the manufacture of your drug products. You also relied on your suppliers' certificates of analysis (COA) for (b)(4) without demonstrating the reliability of your suppliers' test analyses at appropriate intervals. (b)(4) Your incoming inspection records for your (b)(4) active ingredient failed to include appropriate compendial identity testing, assay, or impurity testing. You manufacture drugs that contain (b)(4) . The use of (b)(4) contaminated with (b)(4) has resulted in various lethal poisoning incidents in humans worldwide. See FDA’s guidance document (b)(4). (b)(4) Your incoming inspection records for your (b)(4) component similarly failed to include compendial identity testing and lacked appropriate (b)(4) limit testing. Identity testing for (b)(4) and certain other high-risk drug components includes a limit test in the United States Pharmacopeia (USP) to ensure that the component meets the relevant safety limits for levels of (b)(4) . The use of ingredients contaminated with (b)(4) has resulted in various lethal poisoning incidents in humans worldwide. See FDA’s guidance document (b)(4) (b)(4) Based on the records you provided, you did not perform appropriate (b)(4) testing, including (b)(4) testing, on the (b)(4) used to manufacture your drug products. Your (b)(4) specifications reference the Chinese Pharmacopeia rather than USP for (b)(4) . Without adequate (b)(4) testing, you do not have scientific evidence that the (b)(4) used as a component in your drug product manufacturing conforms to appropriate specifications. Component testing is fundamental to quality. Without adequate testing, you do not have scientific evidence that your components conform to appropriate specifications prior to use in the manufacture of your drug products. As a manufacturer, you have a responsibility to sample, test, and examine drug components before use in production to assure adequate quality. 2. Your firm failed to have, for each batch of drug product, appropriate laboratory determination of satisfactory conformance to final specifications for the drug product, including the identity and strength of each active ingredient, prior to release. Your firm also failed to conduct appropriate laboratory testing, as necessary, for each batch of drug product required to be free of objectionable microorganisms (21 CFR 211.165(a) and 211.165(b)). Based on the records and information you provided, you did not demonstrate that you adequately test your OTC finished drug products prior to release for distribution to the United States. Specifically, the certificate of analyses (COA) that you provided did not include identity, assay, or impurity test results. In addition, the COAs provided also reveal that you lacked appropriate testing for objectionable microorganisms for each batch. Testing is an essential part of CGMP to ensure that the drug products you manufacture conform to all pre-determined quality attributes appropriate for their intended use. Drug products must be tested for identity and strength of the active ingredient prior to release and distribution. Without adequate testing, you do not have scientific evidence to assure that your drug products conform to appropriate specifications before release. 3. Your firm’s quality unit failed to exercise its responsibility to ensure drug products manufactured are in compliance with CGMP and meet established specifications for identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.22). The records and information you provided demonstrate that your quality unit (QU) did not effectively exercise its responsibilities to oversee the quality of your drug manufacturing operations. For example, your QU failed to ensure: The establishment of an adequate, ongoing stability program (21 CFR 211.166(a)). Adequate procedures ensuring appropriate production and process controls, including appropriate qualification of the (b)(4) system (21 CFR 211.100(a)). Your firm’s quality systems are inadequate. For help implementing quality systems and risk management approaches to meet the requirements of CGMP regulations 21 CFR, parts 210 and 211, see FDA’s guidance documents Quality Systems Approach to Pharmaceutical CGMP Regulations at https://www.fda.gov/media/71023/download. CGMP Consultant Recommended Based upon the nature of the violations we identified in your response, you should engage a consultant qualified as set forth in 21 CFR 211.34, to evaluate your operations and to assist your firm in meeting CGMP requirements. The qualified consultant should also perform a comprehensive six-system audit of your entire operation for CGMP compliance and evaluate the completion and efficacy of your corrective actions and preventive actions before you pursue resolution of your firm’s compliance status with FDA. Your use of a consultant does not relieve your firm’s obligation to comply with CGMP. Your firm’s executive management remains responsible for resolving all deficiencies and systemic flaws to ensure ongoing CGMP compliance. Conclusion As previously stated, you are responsible for investigating and determining the root causes of any violations and implementing corrective and preventive measures to ensure future and sustained compliance so that these violations and any others do not occur. FDA placed all drugs and drug products offered for import into the United States from your firm on Import Alert 66-40 on August 7, 2026. FDA may withhold approval of new applications or supplements listing your firm as a drug manufacturer until any violations are completely addressed and we confirm your compliance with CGMP. We may inspect to verify that you have completed corrective actions to any violations. Failure to address any violations may also result in the FDA continuing to refuse admission of articles manufactured at Guangdong Bangze Medicine Co., Ltd., No. 300 Shangfang Avenue, Simapu Town, Chaonan District, Shantou, Guangdong, 515149 China, into the United States under section 801(a)(3) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 381(a)(3). Articles under this authority that appear to be adulterated may be detained or refused admission, in that the methods and controls used in their manufacture do not appear to conform to CGMP within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). Send your written response to CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of this letter. Identify your written response with FEI 3035364398 and ATTN: Christopher Jenner in the subject line of the email. If you have information that you believe demonstrates that your products are not in violation of the FD&C Act and FDA regulations, include that information for our consideration. FDA posts warning letters to www.FDA.gov. Sincerely, /S/ Francis Godwin Director Office of Manufacturing Quality Office of Compliance Center for Drug Evaluation and Research U.S. Food and Drug Administration Cc: Registered U.S. Agent Frosa Technology, LLC (b)(4) Content current as of: 11/03/2026 Regulated Product(s) Drugs Over-the-Counter Drugs Feedback FDA Archive About FDA Accessibility Visitor Information Website Policies / Privacy No FEAR Act Vulnerability Disclosure Policy FOIA HHS.gov USA.gov Contact FDA Follow FDA on Facebook Follow FDA on X Follow FDA on Instagram Follow FDA on LinkedIn View FDA videos on YouTube Subscribe to FDA RSS feeds Contact Number 1-888-INFO-FDA (1-888-463-6332) Back to Top

key_violations.original: 1. Your firm failed to ensure that laboratory records included complete data derived from all tests necessary to ensure compliance with established specifications and standards (21 CFR 211.194(a)). You lacked complete and original laboratory data demonstrating that the required testing was performed. You use (b)(4) as a major component of your drug products. During the inspection, we observed multiple media plates with (b)(4) for (b)(4) samples in your incubator with visible microbiological growth. However, on the next day, during plate reading and result recording, there was no visible microbiological growth on plates labeled as the same samples observed the day before. Additionally, we identified multiple discrepancies between the labeling of the sample identification information handwritten on the exterior of the plates from one day to the subsequent day.
key_violations.description: 1. 귀사는 시험실 기록에 설정된 규격과 기준에 대한 적합성을 보장하는 데 필요한 모든 시험에서 얻은 완전한 데이터가 포함되도록 하지 않았다(21 CFR 211.194(a)). 귀사에는 요구된 시험이 수행되었음을 입증하는 완전한 원본 시험 데이터가 없었다. 귀사는 (b)(4) 를 의약품의 주요 원료로 사용한다. 실사 중 우리는 배양기 안에서 (b)(4) 시료용 (b)(4) 배지 평판 여러 장에 육안으로 보이는 미생물 성장이 있는 것을 관찰했다. 그러나 다음 날 평판 판독과 결과 기록 시점에는 같은 시료로 표시된 평판에서 육안으로 보이는 미생물 성장이 없었다. 또한 평판 바깥면에 손으로 적은 시료 식별 정보가 하루와 그 다음 날 사이에 여러 군데 서로 다르게 표시된 것을 확인했다.
key_violations.risk: 미생물 시험 결과 위조로 오염된 원료·제품이 적합으로 판정돼 아동용 제품까지 유통될 수 있다.

key_violations.original: 2. Your firm failed to conduct at least one test to verify the identity of each component of a drug product. Your firm also failed to validate and establish the reliability of your component supplier’s test analyses at appropriate intervals (21 CFR 211.84(d)(1) and 211.84(d)(2)). You failed to perform adequate identity testing for each component lot used in the production of your OTC drug products. You relied on the certificates of analysis (COAs) from your suppliers and failed to establish the reliability of each of your suppliers’ COA for component specifications and characteristics. Products Contain Ingredients at Risk for Diethylene Glycol or Ethylene Glycol (DEG or EG) Contamination You manufacture multiple toothpaste drug products (intended for adults and children) that contain sorbitol solution. You failed to adequately test your incoming components at high risk of DEG and EG contamination for identity before using them to manufacture your drug products. For example, during the inspection, you provided our investigators with one COA with independent identity testing results, including DEG and EG, out of approximately (b)(4) shipments of sorbitol solution. Identity testing, including DEG and EG, is required for each lot that you receive.
key_violations.description: 2. 귀사는 의약품 각 원료의 확인(identity)을 검증하기 위한 시험을 최소 1개도 실시하지 않았다. 또한 원료 공급업체 시험분석의 신뢰성을 적절한 주기로 검증·확립하지 않았다(21 CFR 211.84(d)(1) 및 211.84(d)(2)). 귀사는 OTC 의약품 생산에 사용한 각 원료 로트에 대해 적절한 확인시험을 하지 않았다. 귀사는 공급업체의 시험성적서(COA)에 의존했고 원료 규격과 특성에 관한 각 공급업체 COA 의 신뢰성을 확립하지 않았다. 디에틸렌글리콜 또는 에틸렌글리콜(DEG 또는 EG) 오염 위험이 있는 성분을 함유한 제품: 귀사는 소르비톨 용액을 함유한 여러 치약 의약품(성인 및 아동용)을 제조한다. 귀사는 DEG·EG 오염 위험이 높은 입고 원료를 의약품 제조에 사용하기 전에 확인시험을 적절히 하지 않았다. 예를 들어 실사 중 귀사가 조사관에게 제시한 것은 약 (b)(4) 회의 소르비톨 용액 입고분 가운데 DEG·EG 를 포함한 독립 확인시험 결과가 있는 COA 1건뿐이었다. DEG·EG 를 포함한 확인시험은 입고되는 모든 로트마다 요구된다.
key_violations.risk: DEG·EG 오염 원료가 확인 없이 치약에 투입되면 치명적 중독 사고로 이어질 수 있다.

key_violations.original: 3. Your firm’s quality control unit failed to exercise its responsibility to ensure drug products manufactured are in compliance with CGMP, and meet established specifications for identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.22). Your QU failed to exercise its authority and responsibilities over your drug manufacturing operations, including ensuring the data integrity of your records. For example, the QU failed to ensure: (b)(4) was suitable for its intended use (21 CFR 211.100). An adequate training program for your microbiology laboratory employees that objectively evaluated competency and proficiency results to assess training effectiveness (21 CFR 211.25(c)). Adequate laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures (21 CFR 211.160(b)).
key_violations.description: 3. 귀사의 품질관리부서는 제조된 의약품이 CGMP 를 준수하고 확인(identity)·함량(strength)·품질(quality)·순도(purity)에 관한 설정 규격을 충족하도록 보장할 책임을 이행하지 않았다(21 CFR 211.22). 귀사 QU 는 기록의 데이터 무결성 보장을 포함하여 의약품 제조 운영에 대한 권한과 책임을 행사하지 않았다. 예를 들어 QU 는 다음을 보장하지 못했다: (b)(4) 가 의도한 용도에 적합한지(21 CFR 211.100). 미생물 시험실 직원의 역량·숙련도 결과를 객관적으로 평가해 교육 효과를 판단하는 적절한 교육 프로그램(21 CFR 211.25(c)). 과학적으로 타당하고 적절한 규격·기준·검체 채취 계획·시험 절차를 포함한 적절한 시험실 관리(21 CFR 211.160(b)).
key_violations.risk: 품질부서의 감독 부재로 용수 시스템·시험실 관리·교육 결함이 방치돼 데이터 신뢰성 전반이 무너진다.

key_violations.original: Based on our review of batch records and product labels, your “Brush Buddies Cookies ‘n Cream Ice Cream Flavored Toothpaste” contains the color additive “CI 14720” (also known as Ext. D&C Red No. 10 or Acid Red No. 14 or Food Red 3 or Carmoisine or Azorubine (E122)). In 1966, FDA cancelled the certification and delisted Ext. D&C Red No. 10 due to lack of safety data from any manufacturer. Under 21 CFR 81.30(d), using Ext. D&C Red No.10 after October 4, 1966, results in the drug being adulterated.
key_violations.description: 배치기록과 제품 라벨을 검토한 결과, 귀사의 “Brush Buddies Cookies ‘n Cream Ice Cream Flavored Toothpaste” 에는 색소 첨가물 “CI 14720”(Ext. D&C Red No. 10, Acid Red No. 14, Food Red 3, Carmoisine 또는 Azorubine(E122)으로도 알려짐)이 함유돼 있다. FDA 는 1966년 어떤 제조업체로부터도 안전성 자료가 없다는 이유로 Ext. D&C Red No. 10 의 인증을 취소하고 목록에서 삭제했다. 21 CFR 81.30(d) 에 따라 1966년 10월 4일 이후 Ext. D&C Red No.10 을 사용하면 그 의약품은 불량의약품(adulterated)이 된다.
key_violations.risk: 아동용 치약에 안전성 미확인 색소가 사용돼 제품 자체가 불량의약품으로 판정된다.

deep_analysis.fda_evaluation: FDA 는 2026년 5월 11일 기록 요청 회신과 6월 25일 483 회신을 검토했다. 미생물 결과 위조에 대해 업체는 평판 바꿔치기를 미생물 담당자의 고의적이지만 단발적인 행위로 결론 내고 재교육, 변조 방지 봉인, 색상 구분, 2인 동시 판독을 도입했다고 했으나, FDA 는 데이터 무결성 위반의 심각성을 다루지 않고 이를 품질부서 감독 붕괴와 품질 문화 결함의 증거가 아닌 개별 절차 공백으로 취급했으며 이미 미국에 유통된 제품 영향 평가도 없다며 불충분하다고 평가했다. DEG·EG 시험에 대해서도 입고 시 확인시험 도입과 보관검체 파괴시험 계획만 제시했을 뿐 소르비톨 용액이 사용 전 확인시험됐다는 추가 증거가 없고 글리세린·폴리에틸렌글리콜 등 다른 고위험 원료를 다루지 않았다는 이유로 불충분하다고 봤다.

required_remediation.deadline: 서한 수령 후 15영업일 이내 서면 회신, DEG·EG 보관검체 시험 결과는 서한일로부터 30일 이내 제출 약속
items: 시험실 관행·절차·장비·문서화·감독·분석자 역량에 대한 독립적 종합 평가와 개선 계획을 제출한다.
미생물 시료의 고유 표시·취급자 서명·시점 기록·판독 시 디지털 사진 등 시료 관리 체계를 컨설턴트 감독 하의 CAPA 로 구축한다.
고위험 원료 전 로트의 보관검체를 DEG·EG 시험하고, 유효기간 내 제품에 대한 위험평가와 필요 시 회수를 실시한다.
제3자 컨설턴트를 통해 데이터 무결성 조사·위험평가·전사 CAPA 관리 전략을 수립한다.

deep_analysis.administrative_risks: FDA 는 2026년 9월 3일 이 업체의 모든 의약품을 Import Alert 66-40 에 등재했고, 업체는 9월 10일 유효기간 내 치약 제품을 자진회수했다. 위반 해소와 CGMP 준수 확인 전까지 이 업체를 제조소로 기재한 신규 신청·변경 승인이 보류될 수 있고, 시정 확인 재실사와 FD&C Act 801(a)(3) 에 따른 반입 거부가 계속될 수 있다.

violations_ko.statement_ko: 귀사는 시험실 기록에 설정된 규격과 기준에 대한 적합성을 보장하는 데 필요한 모든 시험에서 얻은 완전한 데이터가 포함되도록 하지 않았다 (21 CFR 211.194(a)).
귀사는 의약품 각 원료의 확인(identity)을 검증하기 위한 시험을 최소 1개도 실시하지 않았다. 또한 원료 공급업체 시험분석의 신뢰성을 적절한 주기로 검증·확립하지 않았다 (21 CFR 211.84(d)(1) 및 211.84(d)(2)).
귀사의 품질관리부서는 제조된 의약품이 CGMP 를 준수하고 확인(identity)·함량(strength)·품질(quality)·순도(purity)에 관한 설정 규격을 충족하도록 보장할 책임을 이행하지 않았다 (21 CFR 211.22).

142f18a0ab47.source_text: FDA Review Violations were identified and documented during review of your drug manufacturing facility, Pritam International Private Limited, FDA Establishment Identifier (FEI) 3020826443. This review was conducted under FDA’s statutory authority and public health responsibilities to protect the public from unsafe, ineffective, and poor quality drugs. Your facility is registered with the FDA as a manufacturer of over-the-counter (OTC) drug products. FDA has reviewed the records you submitted in response to our April 24, 2026, request for records and other information pursuant to section 704(a)(4) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) for your facility. FDA Inspection Violations were also identified and documented during an inspection of your drug manufacturing facility, Pritam International Private Limited, FEI 3020826443 from June 2 to 6, 2026. This inspection was conducted under FDA’s statutory authority and public health responsibilities to protect the public from unsafe, ineffective, and poor quality drugs. This warning letter summarizes significant violations of Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) regulations for finished pharmaceuticals. See Title 21 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), parts 210 and 211 (21 CFR parts 210 and 211). Because your methods, facilities, or controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding do not conform to CGMP, your drug products are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). In addition, your “Brush Buddies Cookies ‘n Cream Ice Cream Flavored Toothpaste” is adulterated under section 501(a)(4)(A) as this drug product bears or contains a color additive that is unsafe within the meaning of section 721 of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 379e. Accordingly, the introduction or delivery for introduction of “Brush Buddies Cookies ‘n Cream Ice Cream Flavored Toothpaste” into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under section 301(a) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 331(a). We reviewed your May 11, 2026, response to our request for records in detail, and your June 25, 2026, response to our Form FDA 483 in detail and acknowledge receipt of your subsequent correspondence. Violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act The following are violations identified during our inspection and our records review. As a reminder, this is not an all-inclusive list of violations at your facility. Adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(4)(A) of the FD&C Act Your firm contract manufactures OTC toothpaste and (b)(4) drug products for distribution to the U.S. market. Your toothpaste drug products are indicated for use in both children and adults. Based on our review of batch records and product labels, your “Brush Buddies Cookies ‘n Cream Ice Cream Flavored Toothpaste” contains the color additive “CI 14720” (also known as Ext. D&C Red No. 10 or Acid Red No. 14 or Food Red 3 or Carmoisine or Azorubine (E122)). In 1966, FDA cancelled the certification and delisted Ext. D&C Red No. 10 due to lack of safety data from any manufacturer. Under 21 CFR 81.30(d), using Ext. D&C Red No.10 after October 4, 1966, results in the drug being adulterated. Any color additive not explicitly listed as safe for its intended use is deemed unsafe within the meaning of section 721(a) of the FD&C Act. The inclusion of a delisted color additive in your drug product formulation indicates that your quality unit’s review (as required under 21 CFR 211.22) of your raw material qualification process and formulation review procedures are inadequate to ensure that only acceptable ingredients are used in the manufacture of drug products, especially those marketed to children. In response to this letter, provide: A risk assessment to review all your drug formulations to ensure the use of appropriate color additives, including any that may use alternate names. For more information, see the webpage for Regulatory Status of Color Additives at https://www.hfpappexternal.fda.gov/scripts/fdcc/index.cfm?set=ColorAdditives. Adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act 1. Your firm failed to ensure that laboratory records included complete data derived from all tests necessary to ensure compliance with established specifications and standards (21 CFR 211.194(a)). You lacked complete and original laboratory data demonstrating that the required testing was performed. You use (b)(4) as a major component of your drug products. During the inspection, we observed multiple media plates with (b)(4) for (b)(4) samples in your incubator with visible microbiological growth. However, on the next day, during plate reading and result recording, there was no visible microbiological growth on plates labeled as the same samples observed the day before. Additionally, we identified multiple discrepancies between the labeling of the sample identification information handwritten on the exterior of the plates from one day to the subsequent day. Microbiological monitoring and testing are essential quality control steps that are integral to ensure raw materials are adequate for use. Such programs provide critical information on the state of control of the manufacturing operation. Substitution of unreliable or false results fundamentally compromises a facility’s ability to identify risks to the drug product. In your response, you indicate that an investigation into the falsified results concluded that the “… transposition of plates …” was a deliberate but isolated act by the microbiologist to circumvent your procedure. You state that you retrained the microbiologists to recognize when a plate should be considered Too Numerous To Count (TNTC), introduced a tamper evident seal for the plate, implemented color coding to differentiate the negative control plate from the product or component sample, and mandated that all microbiological plate reading must be performed by two analysts concurrently prior to data entry. Your response is inadequate since you fail to address the severity of the observed data integrity violation for the falsification and alteration of the microbiological test results. Your proposed corrective actions address the data integrity breaches as isolated procedural gaps rather than as evidence of a systemic breakdown in quality unit (QU) oversight and a deficient quality culture. Your response does not address the fundamental failure of your QU to ensure the integrity and completeness of all data related to your drug manufacturing operations, nor does it include an adequate assessment of the potential impact on the quality of drug products already distributed to the U.S. market. Furthermore, your response lacks a sufficient comprehensive evaluation of your QU’s capabilities to fulfill all required quality-related functions. Microbiological testing, an essential quality control step, is integral in preventing distribution of unsafe products. Integrity of data is fundamentally compromised when there is a failure to record or maintain complete and accurate records of test results or conditions associated with drug testing. Furthermore, the lack of reliable data compromises the QU’s ability to exercise its function of ensuring compliance with applicable standards. In response to this letter, provide: A comprehensive, independent assessment of your laboratory practices, procedures, methods, equipment, documentation, supervisory oversight, and analyst competencies. Based on this review, provide a detailed plan to remediate and evaluate the effectiveness of your laboratory system. A comprehensive, independent assessment of documentation systems used throughout your manufacturing and laboratory operations to determine where documentation practices are insufficient. Include a detailed Corrective Action and Preventive Action (CAPA) plan that comprehensively remediates your firm’s documentation practices to ensure you retain attributable, legible, complete, original, accurate, contemporaneous (ALCOA) records throughout your operation. A comprehensive CAPA, overseen by a qualified consultant, for handling microbiological sampling media to ensure robust and reliable data. Establish a system that ensures uninterrupted and uncompromised custody, with full reconciliation of all microbiological samples, including but not limited to: o unique labeling of each sample o signatures of all staff who handle the sample o complete tracking of sample integrity and custody o date and time of each activity (e.g., sample collection, transport, delivery, incubation, removal from incubator) o digital time-stamped photos of all plates at the time of plate reading o laboratory tools (e.g., magnification, appropriate light) and methods that optimize visibility and detectability of colonies on plates o signatures of personnel performing reading of microbial counts o provisions for verifications and routine quality assurance oversight 2. Your firm failed to conduct at least one test to verify the identity of each component of a drug product. Your firm also failed to validate and establish the reliability of your component supplier’s test analyses at appropriate intervals (21 CFR 211.84(d)(1) and 211.84(d)(2)). You failed to perform adequate identity testing for each component lot used in the production of your OTC drug products. You relied on the certificates of analysis (COAs) from your suppliers and failed to establish the reliability of each of your suppliers’ COA for component specifications and characteristics. Products Contain Ingredients at Risk for Diethylene Glycol or Ethylene Glycol (DEG or EG) Contamination You manufacture multiple toothpaste drug products (intended for adults and children) that contain sorbitol solution. You failed to adequately test your incoming components at high risk of DEG and EG contamination for identity before using them to manufacture your drug products. For example, during the inspection, you provided our investigators with one COA with independent identity testing results, including DEG and EG, out of approximately (b)(4) shipments of sorbitol solution. Identity testing, including DEG and EG, is required for each lot that you receive. The use of ingredients contaminated with DEG or EG has resulted in various lethal poisoning incidents in humans worldwide. See FDA’s guidance document, Testing of Glycerin, Propylene Glycol, Maltitol Solution, Hydrogenated Starch Hydrolysate, Sorbitol Solution, and Other High-Risk Drug Components for Diethylene Glycol and Ethylene Glycol , to help you meet the CGMP requirements when manufacturing drugs containing ingredients at high-risk for DEG or EG contamination at https://www.fda.gov/media/167974/download. In your response, you proposed modifying the receipt of drums and tanker trucks of the sorbitol solution component to perform identity testing prior to use in manufacturing. You also indicated that you would perform destructive testing of all finished drug product reserve (control) samples. Your response is inadequate. You did not provide any additional evidence that sorbitol solution had been properly tested to confirm identity prior to use. Furthermore, you did not address whether identity testing is performed for other potential high-risk components (such as glycerin and polyethylene glycol). Without appropriate testing of components and ingredients, you cannot ensure the quality and safety of your drug products. Without adequate testing and confirmation of reliability of supplier and external laboratory testing results, you lack scientific evidence that the components or drug products conform to appropriate specifications. In response to this letter, provide: A commitment to provide DEG and EG test results, no later than 30 calendar days from the date of this letter, from testing retains for all lots of high-risk drug components used in the manufacture of drug products. Alternatively, if a retain of a component lot is unavailable, perform retain sample testing of all implicated finished drug product batches for the presence of DEG and EG. A full risk assessment for drug products that are within expiry which contain any ingredient at risk for DEG or EG contamination (including, but not limited to, glycerin). Take prompt and appropriate actions to determine the safety of all lots of the component(s) and any related drug product that could contain DEG or EG, including customer notifications and product recalls for any contaminated lots. Identify additional appropriate CAPA that secure supply chains in the future, including, but not limited to, ensuring that all incoming raw material lots are from fully qualified manufacturers and free from unsafe impurities. Detail these actions in your response to this letter. A description of how you will test each component lot for conformity with all appropriate specifications for identity, strength, quality, and purity. If you intend to accept any results from your supplier’s COA instead of testing each component lot for strength, quality, and purity, specify how you will robustly establish the reliability of your supplier’s results through initial validation as well as periodic revalidation. In addition, include a commitment to always conduct at least one specific identity test for each incoming component lot. In the case of glycerin, propylene glycol, and certain additional high-risk components we note that this includes the performance of parts A, B, and C of the United States Pharmacopeia (USP) monograph. The chemical quality control specifications you use to test each incoming lot of high-risk drug components to determine acceptability for use in manufacturing. A comprehensive, independent review of your material system to determine whether all suppliers of components, containers, and closures, are each qualified and the materials are assigned appropriate expiration or retest dates. The review should also determine whether incoming material controls are adequate to prevent use of unsuitable components, containers, and closures. A summary of results obtained from testing all components to evaluate the reliability of the COA from each component manufacturer. Include your SOP that describes this COA validation program. 3. Your firm’s quality control unit failed to exercise its responsibility to ensure drug products manufactured are in compliance with CGMP, and meet established specifications for identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.22). Your QU failed to exercise its authority and responsibilities over your drug manufacturing operations, including ensuring the data integrity of your records. For example, the QU failed to ensure: (b)(4) was suitable for its intended use (21 CFR 211.100). An adequate training program for your microbiology laboratory employees that objectively evaluated competency and proficiency results to assess training effectiveness (21 CFR 211.25(c)). Adequate laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures (21 CFR 211.160(b)). For help implementing quality system and risk management approaches to meet the requirements of CGMP regulations 21 CFR, parts 210 and 211, see FDA’s guidance documents Quality Systems Approach to Pharmaceutical CGMP Regulations at https://www.fda.gov/media/71023/download, as well as ICH Q10 Pharmaceutical Quality System at https://www.fda.gov/media/71553/download. In response to this letter, provide: A comprehensive assessment and remediation plan to ensure your QU is given the authority and resources to effectively function. The assessment should also include, but not be limited to: o A determination of whether procedures used by your firm are robust and appropriate o Provisions for QU oversight throughout your operations to evaluate adherence to appropriate practices o A complete and final review of each batch and its related information before the QU disposition decision o Oversight and approval of investigations and discharging of all other QU duties to ensure identity, strength, quality, and purity of all products o Also describe how top management supports quality assurance and reliable operations including, but not limited to, timely provision of resources to proactively address emerging quality issues and to assure a continuing state of control. A comprehensive remediation plan for the design, control, and maintenance of the (b)(4) system, including: o A comprehensive evaluation of vulnerabilities of (b)(4) system design and control and summarize all deficiencies found in the system. The summary should, at minimum, describe various system characteristics that were assessed for adequacy (system temperature, materials of construction, slope, any identified dead-legs, any stagnant locations, any unsanitary fittings, flow velocity, etc.) Your total microbiological count limits to monitor whether this system produces (b)(4) suitable for the intended uses for each of your products. A detailed risk assessment addressing the potential effects of the observed (b)(4) system failures on the quality of all drug product lots currently in U.S. distribution. Specify actions that you will take in response to the risk assessment, such as customer notifications and product recalls. CGMP Consultant Recommended Based upon the nature of the violations we identified at your firm, you should engage a consultant qualified as set forth in 21 CFR 211.34 to evaluate your operations and to assist your firm in meeting CGMP requirements if your firm intends to resume manufacturing drugs for the U.S. market. The qualified consultant should also perform a comprehensive six-system audit of your entire operation for CGMP compliance and evaluate the completion and efficacy of your CAPA before you pursue resolution of your firm’s compliance status with FDA. Your use of a consultant does not relieve your firm’s obligation to comply with CGMP. Your firm’s executive management remains responsible for resolving all deficiencies and systemic flaws to ensure ongoing CGMP compliance. Data Integrity Remediation Your quality system does not adequately ensure the accuracy and integrity of data to support the safety, effectiveness, and quality of the drugs you manufacture. See FDA’s guidance document Data Integrity and Compliance With Drug CGMP: Questions and Answers for guidance on establishing and following CGMP compliant data integrity practices at https://www.fda.gov/media/119267/download. We strongly recommend that you retain an independent, qualified third-party consultant to assist in your data integrity remediation. In response to this letter, provide: A comprehensive investigation into the extent of the inaccuracies and inconsistencies in data, records, and reporting. Your investigation should include: o A detailed investigation protocol and methodology; a summary of all laboratories, manufacturing operations, and systems to be covered by the assessment; and a justification for any part of your operation that you propose to exclude. o Interviews of current and former employees to identify the nature, scope, and root cause of data inaccuracies. We recommend that these interviews be conducted by a qualified third party. o An assessment of the extent of data integrity deficiencies at your facility. Identify omissions, alterations, deletions, record destruction, non-contemporaneous record completion, and other deficiencies. Describe all parts of your facility’s operations in which you discovered data integrity deficiencies. o A comprehensive retrospective evaluation of the nature of the testing data integrity deficiencies. We recommend that a qualified third party with specific expertise in the area where potential breaches were identified should evaluate all occurrences. A current risk assessment of the potential effects of the observed failures on the quality of your drugs. Your assessment should include analyses of the risks to patients caused by the release of drugs affected by a data integrity event and analyses of the risks posed by ongoing operations. A management strategy for your firm that includes the details of your global CAPA plan. Your strategy should include: o A detailed corrective action plan that describes how you intend to ensure the reliability and completeness of all data, including analytical data, manufacturing records, and all data submitted to FDA. o A comprehensive description of the root causes of each data integrity deviation, including evidence that the scope and depth of the current action plan is commensurate with the findings of the investigation and risk assessment. Indicate whether individuals responsible for the data integrity breaches remain able to influence CGMP-related or drug application data at your firm. o Interim measures describing the actions you have taken or will take to ensure the quality of your drugs and protect patients, such as notifying your customers, recalling product(s), conducting additional testing, adding lots to your stability programs to assure stability, drug application actions, and enhanced complaint monitoring. o Long-term measures describing any remediation efforts and enhancements to procedures, processes, methods, controls, systems, management oversight, and human resources (e.g., training, staffing improvements) designed to ensure the integrity of your company’s data. o A commitment to have a qualified consultant conduct extensive annual audits, for at least two years, to assist in evaluating CAPA effectiveness after you have executed your data integrity remediation protocol. o Inform FDA if you will be hiring a chief integrity officer who is fully empowered to receive anonymous complaints from employees reporting data integrity concerns and with the authority to ensure any potential breach is promptly investigated (by an independent quality assurance function, along with expertise from outside entities whenever needed). o A status report for any of the above activities already underway or completed. Drug Recall On September 1, 2026, FDA held a teleconference with you recommending you remove your toothpaste drug products within expiry from the U.S. market. On September 10, 2026, you issued a voluntary recall of all toothpaste drug products within expiry that were shipped between September 2024 and August 2026 currently in distribution in the United States. This recall included the “Brush Buddies Cookies ‘n Cream Ice Cream Flavored Toothpaste” that contained a cancelled color additive. The recall was posted to the FDA’s Enforcement Report website at: https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/ires/?Event=99849. Revocation of FD&C Red No. 3 FDA revoked the authorization for the use of FD&C Red No. 3. We recommend manufacturers review their drug product formulations. Manufacturers who use FD&C Red No. 3 in ingested drugs will have until January 18, 2028, to reformulate their products. For more information see https://www.fda.gov/food/hfp-constituent-updates/fda-revoke-authorization-use-red-no-3-food-and-ingested-drugs. Conclusion You are responsible for investigating and determining the root causes of any violations and implementing corrective and preventative measures to ensure future and sustained compliance so that these violations and any others do not occur. FDA placed all drugs and drug products offered for import into the United States from your firm on Import Alert 66-40 on September 3, 2026. FDA may withhold approval of new applications or supplements listing your firm as a drug manufacturer until any violations are completely addressed and we confirm your compliance with CGMP. We may re-inspect to verify that you have completed corrective actions to any violations. Failure to address any violations may also result in the FDA continuing to refuse admission of articles manufactured at Pritam International Private Limited located at Khasra No. 138, Raipur Industrial Area, Bhagwanpur in Haridwar, India into the United States under section 801(a)(3) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 381(a)(3). Articles under this authority that appear to be adulterated may be detained or refused admission, in that the methods and controls used in their manufacture do not appear to conform to CGMP within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). Send your written response to CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of this letter. Identify your written response with FEI 3020826443 and ATTN: Frank Wackes in the subject line of the email. If you have information that you believe demonstrates that your products are not in violation of the FD&C Act and FDA regulations, include that information for our consideration. FDA posts warning letters to www.FDA.gov. key_violations.original: Based on our review of drug product labels, the “ (b)(4) ” contains the color additive “CI 16185” (also known as FD&C Red No. 2 or Amaranth). In 1976, FDA cancelled the certification and delisted FD&C Red No. 2 because it could not be proven safe for use. Under 21 CFR 81.30(j)(1), using FD&C Red No. 2 in drugs after January 28, 1976, results in the drug being adulterated.
key_violations.description: 의약품 라벨 검토 결과, “ (b)(4) ” 에는 색소 첨가물 “CI 16185”(FD&C Red No. 2 또는 Amaranth 로도 알려짐)가 함유돼 있다. FDA 는 1976년 FD&C Red No. 2 가 안전하다는 것이 입증될 수 없어 그 인증을 취소하고 목록에서 삭제했다. 21 CFR 81.30(j)(1) 에 따라 1976년 1월 28일 이후 의약품에 FD&C Red No. 2 를 사용하면 그 의약품은 불량의약품(adulterated)이 된다.
key_violations.risk: 안전성이 입증되지 않은 색소가 든 제품이 유통돼 제품 자체가 불량의약품이 된다.

key_violations.original: Your firm’s quality unit failed to exercise its responsibility to ensure drug products manufactured are in compliance with CGMP and meet established specifications for identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.22). The records and information provided demonstrate that the quality unit (QU) did not effectively exercise its responsibilities to oversee the quality of the drug manufacturing operations. The response includes discrepancies between the color additive on the labeling versus the batch formulation spreadsheet versus the color specified in the certificate of analysis (COA). For example, the labeling for the “ (b)(4) ” listed “CI 16185” (also known as the cancelled color FD&C Red No. 2) as the color additive. However, the separate formulation ingredient information provided listed a second color additive (b)(4) (also known as (b)(4) ) and the COA provided indicated a third distinct color additive, (b)(4) . On July 28, 2026, the FDA sent an electronic request for additional information requesting clarification of these color additive discrepancies. This request went unanswered as did the follow-up electronic request sent on August 5, 2026.
key_violations.description: 귀사의 품질부서는 제조된 의약품이 CGMP 를 준수하고 확인(identity)·함량(strength)·품질(quality)·순도(purity)에 관한 설정 규격을 충족하도록 보장할 책임을 이행하지 않았다(21 CFR 211.22). 제공된 기록과 정보는 품질부서(QU)가 의약품 제조 운영의 품질을 감독할 책임을 효과적으로 수행하지 않았음을 보여준다. 회신 자료에는 라벨상의 색소, 배치 처방 스프레드시트, 시험성적서(COA)에 명시된 색소 사이에 불일치가 있다. 예를 들어 “ (b)(4) ” 의 라벨에는 색소 첨가물로 “CI 16185”(취소된 색소 FD&C Red No. 2 로도 알려짐)가 기재돼 있었다. 그러나 별도로 제공된 처방 성분 정보에는 두 번째 색소 (b)(4)((b)(4) 로도 알려짐)가 기재돼 있었고, 제공된 COA 에는 세 번째의 다른 색소 (b)(4) 가 표시돼 있었다. 2026년 7월 28일 FDA 는 이 색소 불일치에 대한 해명을 요청하는 전자 추가 정보 요청을 보냈다. 이 요청은 회신되지 않았으며, 2026년 8월 5일 보낸 후속 전자 요청도 마찬가지였다.
key_violations.risk: 처방 성분이 문서마다 달라 실제 투입 원료를 특정할 수 없고 품질부서 승인 체계가 기능하지 않는다.

deep_analysis.fda_evaluation: FDA 는 2026년 5월 1일 704(a)(4) 요청에 대해 (b)(4) 가 업체를 대신해 제출한 기록을 검토했다. 취소된 색소가 처방에 포함된 것은 원료 적격성 평가와 처방 검토 절차에 대한 품질부서 검토가 부적절함을 뜻한다고 보았고, 색소 불일치 해명 요청 두 건에 회신이 없었다는 점에서 QU 가 CGMP 운영을 적절히 감독하지 않을 수 있다고 우려했다. 또한 수탁제조소는 제품 소유자와의 계약과 무관하게 생산 의약품의 품질에 책임이 있다고 명시했다.

required_remediation.deadline: 서한 수령 후 15영업일 이내 서면 회신(CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov)
items: QU 가 권한과 자원을 갖고 기능하도록 하는 종합 평가 및 개선 계획(절차 적정성, 배치 최종 검토, 조사 승인 포함)을 제출한다.
최근 3년간 미국 유통 제품의 로트·수량·유효기간 목록과 고객 목록, 제품 소유자와의 품질계약서를 제출한다.
이명을 포함해 모든 의약품 처방의 색소 적정성을 검토하는 위험평가를 수행한다.
미국 유통 중인 해당 배치의 품질·환자안전 위험에 대한 조치 계획(고객 통보, 회수 또는 시장 철수 포함)을 제출한다.

deep_analysis.administrative_risks: 위반이 완전히 해소되고 CGMP 준수가 확인될 때까지 이 업체를 제조소로 기재한 신규 신청·변경 승인이 보류될 수 있고, 시정 확인 실사가 이뤄질 수 있다. 위반을 해소하지 않으면 FD&C Act 801(a)(3) 에 따라 이 업체 제조품의 미국 반입이 거부될 수 있으며, 불량으로 보이는 제품은 억류되거나 반입이 거부될 수 있다.

630b3e9f64ec.source_text: FDA Review Violations were identified and documented during review of your drug manufacturing facility, Guangzhou Jiugong Research And Development Biotechnology Co., Ltd., FDA Establishment Identifier (FEI) 3043646847. This review was conducted under FDA’s statutory authority and public health responsibilities to protect the public from unsafe, ineffective, and poor quality drugs. Your facility is registered with the FDA as a manufacturer of over-the-counter (OTC) drug products, including (b)(4) . FDA has reviewed the records submitted from (b)(4) on your behalf in response to our May 1, 2026, request for records and other information pursuant to section 704(a)(4) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) for your facility. This warning letter summarizes significant violations of Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) regulations for finished pharmaceuticals. See Title 21 Code of Federal Regulations, parts 210 and 211 (21 CFR, parts 210 and 211). Because your methods, facilities, or controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding of drugs as described in your response to our 704(a)(4) request do not conform to CGMP, your drug products are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B)). Additionally, the OTC drug product, “ (b)(4) ,” is adulterated under section 501(a)(4)(A) as this drug product bears or contains a color additive that is unsafe within the meaning of section 721 of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 379e. Accordingly, the introduction or delivery for introduction of “ (b)(4) ” into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under section 301(a) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 331(a). Violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act The following are violations identified during our review. As a reminder, this is not an all-inclusive list of violations at your facility. Use of Cancelled Color Additive FD&C Red No. 2 Based on our review of drug product labels, the “ (b)(4) ” contains the color additive “CI 16185” (also known as FD&C Red No. 2 or Amaranth). In 1976, FDA cancelled the certification and delisted FD&C Red No. 2 because it could not be proven safe for use. Under 21 CFR 81.30(j)(1), using FD&C Red No. 2 in drugs after January 28, 1976, results in the drug being adulterated. Any color additive not explicitly listed as safe for its intended use is deemed unsafe within the meaning of section 721(a) of the FD&C Act. The inclusion of a delisted color additive in your drug product formulation indicates that your quality unit’s review (as required under 21 CFR 211.22) of your raw material qualification process and formulation review procedures is inadequate. Your firm’s quality unit failed to exercise its responsibility to ensure drug products manufactured are in compliance with CGMP and meet established specifications for identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.22). The records and information provided demonstrate that the quality unit (QU) did not effectively exercise its responsibilities to oversee the quality of the drug manufacturing operations. The response includes discrepancies between the color additive on the labeling versus the batch formulation spreadsheet versus the color specified in the certificate of analysis (COA). For example, the labeling for the “ (b)(4) ” listed “CI 16185” (also known as the cancelled color FD&C Red No. 2) as the color additive. However, the separate formulation ingredient information provided listed a second color additive (b)(4) (also known as (b)(4) ) and the COA provided indicated a third distinct color additive, (b)(4) . On July 28, 2026, the FDA sent an electronic request for additional information requesting clarification of these color additive discrepancies. This request went unanswered as did the follow-up electronic request sent on August 5, 2026. Your QU is responsible for fully exercising its authority and responsibilities. FDA is concerned that your QU may not be conducting appropriate oversight regarding CGMP operations. In response to this letter, provide: A comprehensive assessment and remediation plan to ensure your QU is given the authority and resources to effectively function. The assessment should also include, but not be limited to, the following: o A determination of whether procedures used by your firm are robust and appropriate. o Provisions for QU oversight throughout your operations to evaluate adherence to appropriate practices. o A complete and final review of each batch and its related information before the QU disposition decision. o Oversight and approval of investigations and discharging of all other QU duties to ensure identity, strength, quality, and purity of all products. A comprehensive assessment of your documentation to ensure you retain accurate records throughout your operation. A list of all products distributed in the United States in the last three years, with lot number, quantity shipped, and expiry dates. Identify the drug products you distributed. A list of your customers and addresses where the drug products were distributed. A copy of your quality agreement with the product owner, (b)(4) . A risk assessment to review all your drug formulations to ensure the use of appropriate color additives, including any that may use alternate names. For more information, see the webpage for Regulatory Status of Color Additives at https://www.hfpappexternal.fda.gov/scripts/fdcc/index.cfm?set=ColorAdditives. Your action plan to address any product quality or patient safety risks for batches of (b)(4) in U.S. distribution, including customer notifications and recalls or market withdrawals. Responsibilities as a Contractor You are responsible for the quality of drugs you produce as a contract facility regardless of agreements in place with product owners. You are required to ensure that drugs are made in accordance with section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act for safety, identity, strength, quality, and purity. See FDA’s guidance document Contract Manufacturing Arrangements for Drugs: Quality Agreements at https://www.fda.gov/media/86193/download. Revocation of FD&C Red No. 3 FDA revoked the authorization for the use of FD&C Red No. 3. We recommend manufacturers review their drug product formulations. Manufacturers who use FD&C Red No. 3 in ingested drugs will have until January 18, 2028, to reformulate their products. For more information, see https://www.fda.gov/food/hfp-constituent-updates/fda-revoke-authorization-use-red-no-3-food-and-ingested-drugs. Cosmetics Manufactured for Distribution in the United States In addition, some of the products you manufacture may be regulated as cosmetics, as defined in section 201(i) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 321(i)). Any cosmetics you manufacture must comply with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements, including the FD&C Act. We note that under section 301(a) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 331(a)), it is a prohibited act to introduce or deliver for introduction into interstate commerce a cosmetic that is adulterated or misbranded. We also note that the Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022 (MoCRA) provides new requirements with which facilities that manufacture cosmetic products must comply. You may find the FD&C Act, MoCRA, and FDA’s regulations through links on FDA’s website at www.fda.gov. Conclusion As previously stated, you are responsible for investigating and determining the root causes of any violations and implementing corrective and preventative measures to ensure future and sustained compliance so that these violations and any others do not occur. FDA may withhold approval of new applications or supplements listing your firm as a drug manufacturer until any violations are completely addressed and we confirm your compliance with CGMP. We may inspect to verify that you have completed corrective actions to any violations. Failure to address any violations may also result in the FDA refusing admission of articles manufactured at Guangzhou Jiugong Research And Development Biotechnology Co., Ltd., located at No. 3 Yiheng Road, Nanling Gongye Districtqinghu Ma Tian Street, Jiahe Street, Baiyun District, Guangzhou, Guangdong into the United States under section 801(a)(3) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 381(a)(3). Articles under this authority that appear to be adulterated may be detained or refused admission, in that the methods and controls used in their manufacture do not appear to conform to CGMP within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). Send your written response to CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of this letter. Identify your written response with FEI 3043646847 and ATTN: Lynnsey Renn in the subject line of the email. If you have information that you believe demonstrates that your products are not in violation of the FD&C Act and FDA regulations, include that information for our consideration. FDA posts warning letters to www.FDA.gov.
